newsitem.title: HONG KONG: UK's Cook urges free and fair Hong Kong elections.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook urges free and fair Hong Kong elections.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has urged Hong Kong's future ruler to hold free and fair elections and said on Sunday Chinese troops should not be seen on the streets of Hong Kong.
"The people of Hong Kong have now had a taste of democracy. It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," he told reporters.

Cook, who met Hong Kong's future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa on the Royal Yacht Britannia on Saturday night, said that he pressed him to ensure that "elections should not just be held but be held on a free and fair basis".

"China has given an undertaking that there will be elections within 12 months. That was repeated to me yesterday by C.H. Tung ... This is probably the single biggest issue as a test of good faith," Cook said.
After Monday night's handover ceremonies, Cook and Prime Minister Tony Blair have decided to boycott the swearing-in of a new provisional legislature handpicked by Beijing.
It replaces a legislature democratically elected under reforms instituted by departing British governor Chris Patten, who was vilified by Beijing.

On arriving in Hong Kong on Saturday, Cook attacked as "unnecessary and inappropriate" China's decision to send in 4,000 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops in warships, helicopters and armoured cars just hours after the handover.
On Sunday, Cook said China was within its rights to deploy troops in Hong Kong to protect the territory from attack.

"The internal security of Hong Kong is a matter for the Hong Kong government and its police authorities. It is not a matter for the PLA. Any PLA units deployed here for external defence should be stationed in their barracks or around the perimeter but should not be seen on the streets of Hong Kong."
Cook has urged China to live up to its pledges to preserve Hong Kong's freedoms and way of life or face the prospect of Britain taking the matter to the United Nations.
He pointed to strong statements of support issued after the Denver summit of the Group of Seven industrialised nations as well as the Amsterdam summit of the European Union states.
"Having put down those markers, we now have a very clear basis to go back to the international community to call up their support in the event that it is needed," he said.

Chief executive-designate Tung is unable to attend Britain's sunset farewell ceremony because he will be greeting China's President Jiang Zemin, but Cook denied suggestions that the end-of-empire arrangements had become "scratchy and irritable".
